questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: What libraries are and why they have been important in history
How to get a library card in London
Why people today are reading fewer and fewer books than in the past
How crime novels are written
questions.why: They look into the hidden life of the library, including the Great Library of Alexandria.

questions.q: What is Beth's first idea of what a library is?
options: A place of political power
A museum full of very old and valuable manuscripts
A shop that sells books
A place with lots of books where you read or study
questions.why: She says it's somewhere with lots of books, where you go to read or study.

questions.q: Which of these does Neil say a library can be?
options: A place to buy cheap food
A place to keep warm in winter
A place to watch films
A place to meet famous authors
questions.why: He lists a symbol of knowledge, a place to keep warm in winter, or a crime-novel setting.

questions.q: How does Professor Andrew Pettegree define a library?
options: A public building that is owned by the local government
A collection of at least 1,000 books
Any collection of books that someone chose to build
A place where books can be borrowed for free
questions.why: He says a library is any collection of books deliberately put together by its owner or patron.

questions.q: Why does Pettegree mention two shelves of paperbacks at home?
options: To say that paperbacks are not real books
To complain that people don't read enough
To show that even a small personal collection can be a library
To explain how libraries slowly lost their power and importance over time
questions.why: He uses it as an example of a library, alongside 30 manuscripts in the 15th century.

questions.q: What was different about books in earlier centuries?
options: They were rare and collected slowly with great effort
They were sold cheaply everywhere, even in train stations
They were cheaper than today
They were only written in Egypt
questions.why: Neil says books were rare and may have been painfully collected over many years.

questions.q: What was the aim of the Great Library of Alexandria?
options: To teach soldiers how to fight
To sell books to people across the ancient world
To keep books away from ordinary people
To collect a copy of every book that existed
questions.why: Its mission was to bring together a copy of every book then in existence.

questions.q: According to Professor Islam Issa, how did the library make Alexandria powerful?
options: It paid for the city's army
It showed Alexandria was a centre of knowledge
It attracted rich tourists who spent lots of money
It kept knowledge secret from enemies
questions.why: He says knowledge equals power, and the library was a form of soft power.
